titleStmt.title: Probabilistic Schedulability Analysis for Fault Tolerant Tasks under Stochastic Error Occurrences

analytic.title: Probabilistic Schedulability Analysis for Fault Tolerant Tasks under Stochastic Error Occurrences

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In dependable real-time systems, provision of schedulability guarantees for task sets under realistic fault and error assumptions is an essential requirement, though complex and tricky to achieve. An important factor to be considered in this context is the random nature of occurrences of faults and errors, which, if addressed in the traditional schedulability analysis by assuming a rigid worst case occurrence scenario, may lead to inaccurate results.

In this paper we first propose a stochastic fault and error model which has the capability of modeling error bursts in lieu of the commonly used simplistic error assumptions in processor scheduling. We then present a novel schedulability analysis that accounts for a range of worst case scenarios generated by stochastic error burst occurrences on the response times of tasks scheduled under the fixed priority scheduling (FPS) policy. Finally, we describe a methodology for the calculation of probabilistic schedulability guarantees as a weighted sum of the conditional probabilities of schedulability under specified error burst characteristics.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Embedded systems typically used in real-time (RT) safety critical applications have the major design objective to guarantee the properties of correctness and timeliness even under error occurrences. These systems typically work in harsh environments where they are exposed to frequent transient faults, such as power supply jitter, network noise or radiation, and are often characterized by high reliability requirements that have to be satisfied by using appropriate fault tolerance (FT) techniques. However, the fundamental requirement for the design of effective and efficient FT mechanisms is a realistic and applicable model of potential faults, their manifestations and consequences.

In a large number of safety or mission critical systems, that typically employ the the preemptive fixed priority scheduling (FPS) policy, RT schedulability analysis techniques have been increasingly used in order to ensure that the strict timeliness requirements of the applications are met. Such analysis techniques are typically extended with appropriate error models to provide RT guarantees for fault tolerant systems. Since no real-world systems can cope with an arbitrary number of faults over a bounded interval of time, one has to make realistic and acceptable fault assumptions for the specific context. The majority of the previous research works assumed a worst case error distribution, e.g., single faults with a minimum inter-arrival time equal or greater than the largest period in the task set [14,17,10,6,15,9]. Many of these approaches either did not hold under tighter error assumptions or did not provide information on how better they perform under more relaxed assumptions.

RT scheduling research typically tries to provide worst case guarantees. In cases where it is not possible to derive a worst case property, one looks for potential bounds in order to keep the scheduling guarantees valid, although providing somewhat pessimistic results. However, in the case of fault and error events, such bounds may not exist due to the random nature of such events, and assuming a worst case behaviour may either provide inaccurate or excessively pessimistic analysis results. Hence, it is advisable to combine the analysis with probabilistic argumentations. Burns et al. [7] proposed a probabilistic schedulability approach based on error assumptions modeled as stochastic events, however, they ignored the fact that once an error occurs, it is likely that the fault causing this error will be in effect for a certain duration, causing more errors during that period which can have an adverse effect on the task response times. Note that the concept of error bursts are fairly old, e.g., Burton and Sullivan defined error bursts consisting of errors that are occurring during the period that a fault is in effect and if two successive errors within that duration does not exceed a certain maximum error-free period [8]. Punnekkat et al. [16] proposed an approach to schedule RT messages on CAN in a fault tolerant manner using FPS under a deterministic error model that was capable of modeling error bursts. Navet et al. [13] proposed a probabilistic schedu-lability analysis for message scheduling on CAN. Later on, Broster et al. [3,4,5] addressed the reliability of message transmission on CAN assuming probabilistic error models. Both Navet et al. and Broster et al. presented stochastic error models where they model error bursts as a number of errors within a given time interval. However, they did not model the important characteristics of error bursts such as burst length and the error intensity within a burst, which are crucial for performing more accurate schedulability analyses. Many and Doose [12] presented an error burst model and provided recovery strategies in FPS under error bursts. However their model assumes that a task instance is hit by at most one burst during its execution.

In this paper, we propose a probabilistic schedulability analysis for RT tasks scheduled under the FPS policy using a fault and error model that is capable of modeling error bursts with random attributes. The proposed analysis introduces significant improvements over our earlier work [2] in many aspects, including a major revision of the earlier analysis improving its accuracy and a more elaborate and realistic error model that relaxes the previous assumptions. In particular, we have relaxed the error assumptions so that each burst that occurs during a task's execution can have a random length rather than a random upper bound for all the bursts, as assumed in [2]. Moreover, we revised the expression for calculating the worst case error overhead in two aspects: (1) we solve an issue where, in rare scenarios, the analysis presented in [2] could provide optimistic values of the worst case error overhead, and (2) we reduce the pessimism in the results from the earlier approach, by providing a tighter upper bound on the worst case error overhead calculations. In particular, we provide a more accurate calculation of the worst case error overhead taking into account the relation between the burst length and the WCETs of the primary and the alternate versions of the tasks.

The rest of the paper is organized as following: In Sections 2 and 3, we introduce the task and the error model respectively, followed by the proposed methodology in Section 4. In Section 5 we illustrate our methodology with an example followed by Section 6 which concludes the paper.

div.head: Real-time task model
div.p: We assume a sporadic task set, Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ N }, scheduled by the preemptive FPS paradigm where each task represents a RT thread of execution. Each task τ i has a minimum inter-arrival time T i , a known worst case execution time (WCET) C i , a deadline D i and a unique priority P i . We assume a single processor platform and that the tasks have deadlines equal to or less than their minimum inter arrival times.

We assume that, whenever an error is detected within a task, the affected task τ i executes an alternate task τ alt i with a WCET, C alt i , less than or equal to the original WCET of its primary C i , a deadline equal to the original deadline D i and a minimum inter-arrival time equal to the minimum inter arrival time T i . This alternate can typically be a reexecution of the same task, a recovery block, an exception handler, or an alternate task with imprecise computations. We assume that errors are detected just before the completion of the affected task instances. Although somewhat pessimistic, this assumption is realistic since in many implementations, errors are detected by acceptance tests, which are performed at the end of task executions or by watchdog timers that interrupt the task once it has exhausted its budgeted WCET. In case of tasks communicating via shared resources, we assume that an acceptance test is executed before passing an output value to another task to avoid error propagations and subsequent domino effects.

div.head: Fault and error model
div.p: We assume that the main sources of errors are electromagnetic interferences (external faults), and transient hardware faults (internal faults) that affect, e.g. the sensors and the network systems, resulting in incorrect input values from sensors, or failure in delivering the output values via network messages.

Our fault and error model uses the following three parameters as illustrated in Fig. 1: riods as in the vehicle example which passes through a field with strong electromagnetic interference. The duration of the faults is very much domain specific, and, in this paper, we assume that the information regarding the probability distribution of the fault durations (in the form of error burst lengths) is available. 2. T E : The error rate per unit time λ together with the mission time L of a system determines the minimum inter arrival time T E between two independent faults materializing into either error bursts or single errors with a certain probability. One should note that the mission time L varies largely depending on the domain, typically ranging from minutes for a car to take a short trip to years for a satellite to complete its mission. Furthermore the number of error events in a unit time λ not only depends on the system but also on the type of environment.

div.head: T burst E
div.p: : The intensity of a fault together with various other factors, such as the resistance of the hardware to the fault, and the existing fault detection and FT mechanisms, determine the likelihood that a fault materializes into an error. Hence the combination of these factors determines the minimum inter arrival time between two errors within a burst (T burst E ) with a certain probability. In this paper we assume that no task can successfully finish between errors within a burst. Furthermore, any task instance scheduled even partially under the error burst will be considered as affected by the error. The probability mass function for the error burst lengths is denoted by f (l). This function gives the probabilities of all possible burst lengths from the range of l.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: Our research goal is to find the probability that the given task set is schedulable during a mission time L under the specified error model. This probability is dependent on the error characteristics (the minimum inter arrival time between bursts, T E , the possible values for the burst length l j , and the probability distribution f (l)) and can be derived from the conditional probabilities that the task set is schedulable under specific sets of values for these parameters.

The analysis begins with finding the maximum number of error bursts, n, that can hit any task instance in the task set. Considering the interplay between T E and l j , a set of sensitivity analyses is performed to derive the minimum inter-arrival times between error bursts (T E ) for each possible combination of n burst lengths by assuming the worst case task executions and error overheads. One should note that the derived minimum inter-arrival times are actually upper bounds which may never be reached. This is due to the nature of the inexact worst case assumptions, such as the WCETs of the tasks, which correspond to upper bounds rather than exact worst case values. The burst length combinations and the corresponding upper bound T E values are then used to find the conditional probabilities of schedulability which are lower bounds for the actual probabilities. Finally, a lower bound probability of schedulability is computed as a cumulative sum of these individual conditional lower bound probabilities, i.e. by unconditioning the probability of schedulability with respect to the burst lengths.

STEP 1: We begin the analysis by finding an upper bound for the maximum number of error bursts that can hit any task instance in the task set while the task set is still guaranteed to be schedulable. We assume that all bursts have the shortest possible length and perform a sensitivity analysis to derive the maximum number of bursts that can hit the task with the longest deadline.

STEP 2: In this step, we perform a set of sensitivity analyses for each combination of n burst lengths specified in the probability mass function f (l) in order to derive the minimum inter arrival time between bursts (T E ) under which the task set is still schedulable.

STEP 3: The goal of this step is to derive the probabilities that the actual inter arrival times between bursts will not be shorter than the calculated minimum inter arrival times. We use the previously proposed statistical approaches to find the probability of bursts occurring with inter arrival times larger than or equal to the T E by taking into account λ and the mission time L.
STEP 4: Finally, based on the probability mass function f (l), as well as the derived probabilities for each burst length combination, we derive the cumulative probability of schedulability.

div.head: Worst case response time analysis under error bursts
div.p: In this subsection, we propose a worst case response time analysis (RTA) that identifies whether a given task set is schedulable when affected by error bursts of random length and a minimum inter arrival time T E . One should note that if the burst length is greater than or equal to the minimum inter arrival time between bursts, every burst can start before the end of the previous one, hence the bursts can potentially affect the whole mission time. If this is the case, or if the burst length is greater than the minimum inter arrival time of the task whose worst case response time is to be calculated, the schedulability of this task cannot be guaranteed.
The traditional RTA calculates the worst case response time R i for each task τ i using the following equation assuming that there are no errors and, hence, no recovery attempts [11]:
div.formula: R i = C i + B i + j∈hp(i) R i T j C j (1
div.p: where hp(i) is the set of higher priority tasks than task τ i , B i is the maximum blocking time caused by the concurrency protocols used for accessing the shared resources. The last term is the interference from the higher priority tasks experienced by task τ i , denoted by I hp i . If the worst case response time R i becomes greater than the deadline D i , then the task cannot be guaranteed to meet its deadline, and the task set is therefore considered unschedulable.

If we assume a fault tolerant scheduler, where the tasks affected by errors are re-executed, then the execution of task τ i will interfere with both errors as well as higher priority tasks. Accordingly, the worst case response times are computed [6] by using the following equation:
div.formula: R i = C i +B i + j∈hp(i) R i T j C j + R i T E max k∈hep(i) (F k ) (2)
div.p: where F k is the extra computation time needed by task τ k to recover from the errors, T E is a known minimum inter arrival time between errors, and hep(i) is the set of tasks with priority equal to or higher than the priority of task τ i (hep(i) = hp(i) ∪ τ i ). The last term calculates the worst case interference arising from the recovery attempts and is denoted by I err i . This equation is also solved by a recurrence relation as in the previous case. If all R i values are less than or equal to the corresponding D i values, then the task set is guaranteed to be scheduled under the condition that no two errors occur closer than the T E value.
The main differences between the error characteristics in the traditional single error model and our burst model are:

1. An error burst may consist of multiple errors 2. An error burst may affect multiple tasks Hence, the worst case scenario required for calculating the worst case response times is not the same in case of error bursts as compared to the model introduced in [7].

We denote the set of bursts interfering with a task τ i , i.e., arriving after the release of τ i , by {β j j = 1, 2, ..., n}. Definition 1. We define the worst case error overhead E j i for a task τ i caused by an error burst β j as the largest amount of time required by the task alternates τ alt k , τ k ∈ Γ, to recover from the effects of burst β j , in the interval between the release time of task τ i and its completion.

Remark 1. An important observation is that, while the worst case error overhead accounts for all the alternates required for recovery (including the successful ones), it excludes all the primaries, since, although affected by errors, those are already taken into account in the traditional part of the RTA, i.e., C i and j∈hp(i) Ri Tj C j .

div.p: If a burst hits a task τ i , where i gives the priority level of the task, its worst case error overhead occurs under the following three conditions:

1. the burst starts before the completion of τ i and ends after the start of execution of the last failed execution, 2. the burst hits all tasks with higher priority than τ i , if any, 3. τ i alt and all its higher priority tasks are preempted by their respective next higher priority task (if any), after their start of execution.

Proof. The basic idea is that the burst, in order to cause the most damage, should leave outside its length as much wasted computations as possible. The first condition is a direct result of the Remark 2 and Lemma 4.1. In this case, the largest amount of wasted computation on task τ i outside the burst occurs when the burst hits τ i before its completion and ends right after the start of the last failed execution. Now, in order to maximize the damage, the burst should hit as many tasks as possible during its occurrence, since each additional task hit by the burst will eventually recover and, hence, contribute with at least one extra successful alternate (except the failed ones) to the worst case error overhead. The maximum number of tasks the burst can hit in addition to τ i is given by all higher priority tasks than τ i (proving condition 2). This scenario, in its turn, is only possible if all higher priority tasks preempt each other in increasing priority order, and all preemption points occur during the burst. Additionally, in order to leave as much wasted computation as possible outside the burst. i.e., after the end of the burst, all preemptions should occur as early as possible during the affected tasks' executions.

div.head: Derivation of the probabilistic schedulability bound
div.p: In this paper, we make an assumption similar to the one in [7] that, during a mission, if the actual shortest interval between two error bursts W is less than the derived minimum inter arrival time of error bursts T E , then the task set is unschedulable. Hence, the probability of unschedulability P r(U ), is equal to P r(W < T E ), and our ultimate goal to find the probability of schedulability of a given task set is translated to the derivation of the probability that, during the mission time L, no two consecutive error bursts arrive with an inter arrival time shorter than the derived T E .

We use the following equations, proposed by Burns et al. [7], for the upper and lower bounds of P r(W < T E ). These equations are derived assuming a Poisson probability distribution to find the probability of a number of events that occurs in a fixed time period, provided that the occurrence rate (λ) is constant and the events are independent.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Design of dependable RTS demands advances in both dependability modeling and scheduling theory in tandem, to provide system level guarantees that potential error scenarios are addressed in an effective as well as efficient manner. In this paper, we have introduced a burst error model together with the associated schedulability analysis for dependable RTS. We presented a sufficient analysis that accounts for the worst case interference caused by error bursts on the response times of tasks scheduled under the preemptive FPS policy using a stochastic fault and error model that is capable of modeling error bursts with random attributes. The proposed analysis introduces significant improvements over existing works in many aspects, including a more elaborate and realistic error model and a major revision of earlier analysis achieving higher accuracy. Further, we have outlined a method to derive probabilistic scheduling guarantees from the stochastic behaviour of errors by performing a joint schedulability-and sensitivity analysis.
